RSI ladder: every rung from 1% to 100%, what came next, and every pullback

Statistics · 28 Sep 2026 · built 2026-09-28 13:58 UTC · RSI(14), Wilder, daily closes · data to 2026-09-25 (Bitcoin 2026-09-27) · 26 instruments · research questions, not buy rules · nothing here predicts
STATUS · computed from real daily bars; no fixed zones anywhere. No “bottom 10%”, no “20 sessions” window: every RSI percentile from 1 to 100 is shown, every pullback is listed one by one, and waits are followed to the end (or marked still open). Green = up / better than any day, red = down / worse. “Middle result” = the median. The “90% band” shows how sure a number is: if the any-day number sits inside it, the difference may be luck.

The answers you asked for

  1. The ladder, rung by rung (SPY, 2004–2026). The lowest 1% of days closed with an RSI of 28.3 or lower, the lowest 2% at 31.0, 3% at 32.8, 5% at 35.2, 10% at 39.4, 25% at 46.7; the middle day 56.1; the top 10% from 68.4, top 5% from 71.4, top 1% from 76.7. Every rung from 1 to 100, for all 26 instruments, is in section 1. Visits: SPY dropped to rung 1 or lower 29 separate times (1.3 a year) and each stay was short (typically 2 days, longest 4); to rung 5 or lower 5.1 times a year.
  2. Yes — Bitcoin's RSI goes deeper, and more often. Same years (2013–2026), each on its own days: Bitcoin's bottom 1% is an RSI of 23.3 against SPY's 28.7 and QQQ's 29.6; bottom 5% 32.2 vs 35.8; its middle day 51.6 vs 57.2. Bitcoin sits lower at every rung from 1 to 83. Counted in days: SPY's bottom-1% level (28.3) is reached on 2.4% of Bitcoin days — 2.4 times as often as SPY itself — and SPY's bottom-5% level (35.2) on 8.2% of Bitcoin days (1.6 times). It also runs hotter at the very top: Bitcoin's top 1% starts at 86.3 against SPY's 77.5. The one record that matches Bitcoin's floor is the S&P 500 since 1928, crash years included (bottom 1% 23.9; Bitcoin reaches that level on 1.1% of its days). Reading Bitcoin on weekdays only changes nothing (bottom 1% 23.2).
  3. What came next, rung by rung: no single rung clears luck by much, but the slope is there for most stock funds since 2003 — flat on the S&P since 1928, and reversed for Bitcoin. SPY's rung 1 was followed 20 sessions later by a middle result of +3.1% (90% band +0.6% to +4.8%) against +1.3% on any day; rung 100 by -1.0%. Of SPY's 100 rungs only 6 beat any day beyond their band at 20 sessions and 8 fell short (60 sessions: 7 and 3) — about what luck gives with 90% bands (5 each way). Pooled over all 26 instruments: 207 above and 200 below out of 2600 rungs at 20 sessions (luck alone ≈ 130 each way) — more than luck, but about equally on both sides, which points to bands that are a little too narrow on thin rungs rather than to an edge at the bottom. The pattern shows in the slope instead: ranking the 100 rungs by their middle 20-session result, 15 of 16 stock funds lean the same way — the lower the rung, the better (rank correlation SPY -0.50, IWM -0.63, XLF -0.45); the S&P index since 1928 shows almost none (-0.09); Bitcoin is the opposite (0.43): its high rungs were followed by more gains, its low rungs by less. VIX is the strongest of all (-0.89): a high VIX RSI was usually followed by a falling VIX.
  4. The deeper the RSI, the deeper the next dip first. After SPY's rung-1 days the worst close inside the next 60 sessions was typically -4.0% (any day -3.0%); IWM -6.3% vs -4.4%; Bitcoin -12.2% vs -10.1%; oil -21.5% vs -8.4%. And from a rung-1 day SPY needed a middle 132 sessions to trade back above its prior swing high (any day: 3; partly by construction — an oversold day is usually well under the last top).
  5. Every pullback, as a continuous spread: deeper takes longer, and in the stock indexes nearly every one has already ended in a new high. SPY had 125 pullbacks (10/10 swing pivots) and 125 of 125 traded back above the old top. Half of all of them did so within 18 sessions of the low; the deeper half within 34; the deepest quarter within 91; the deepest tenth within 131. Depth and wait move together (rank correlation 0.60; S&P since 1928 0.63, Bitcoin 0.65). Across S&P 500, SPY, Nasdaq 100, QQQ, IWM, DIA: 1335 of 1336 pullbacks have made a new high (the 1 still open began in 2026). The waits can be very long: the S&P's longest, from the 1929-09-16 top, took 25 years (new high 1954-09-22); the Nasdaq 100's, from 2000-03-24, 16.4 years. Among the sectors only XLRE from 2021-12, XLRE from 2022-04 are still under a pre-2026 top. Outside stocks "it always bounces back" does not hold on price: oil is still under its 2008 top, the 10-year yield under its 1981 top, and 20 TLT pullbacks since 2020 are still open.
  6. S9's "81% / 70% / 25% new high on the next leg", restated without the next-leg cut-off. S9 only asked whether the VERY NEXT rally beat the old top: on SPY that happened 64.8% of the time overall. Allowing as many rallies as it takes, 100.0% got there. For SPY's pullbacks of 10% or more (S9's two deepest bins, 28 of them), the next leg made it only 25.0% of the time, yet all of them eventually did; the middle one took 99 sessions from the low and needed 3 rallies. Section 3 draws this as time-to-new-high curves.
  7. Where each one sits today (close of 2026-09-25, rung of its own full history): lowest — XLU rung 1 (RSI 24.1), XLRE rung 1 (RSI 24.1), TLT rung 5 (RSI 31.6), XLF rung 5 (RSI 32.9), IWM rung 6 (RSI 34.9), XLY rung 11 (RSI 38.7), XLB rung 11 (RSI 38.0); highest — 10y yield rung 96 (RSI 75.3), Dollar rung 91 (RSI 67.2), XLK rung 81 (RSI 65.4), SMH rung 79 (RSI 62.7). Utilities and real estate are on their bottom rung while the 10-year yield sits near its top. These are research observations, not signals.

1 · The ladder: RSI at every rung, 1% to 100%

A rung is one percent of an instrument's own days, ranked by RSI. Rung 1 = the most oversold 1% of all its days; rung 100 = the most overbought 1%. The strip below shows all 26 instruments at once; the outlined cell is where the latest close sits.

Does Bitcoin's RSI go deeper?

Yes, at every rung below about 83, and it also runs hotter at the very top. Same years for all three lines; the bar chart shows the gap to SPY one rung at a time.

Every instrument, all 100 rungs (click a row)

Each row opens three 10×10 grids — full history, last 3 years, and how many separate visits a year it makes at or below each rung — plus its gap to SPY rung by rung.

2 · What came next, at every rung

Every day is placed on its rung, then followed forward: the change 5, 10, 20 and 60 sessions later, the share of days that ended higher, the worst close in the next 20 and 60 sessions, and the wait until price traded back above the last swing high that was already confirmed that day. Each dot is one rung; its faint bar is the 90% band; the dashed line is any day. “Rungs above / below” counts how many of the 100 rungs cleared the any-day number beyond their band — with 90% bands about 5 each way happen by luck alone.

3 · Every pullback, one by one

A pullback runs from a swing high to the next swing low (S9's rule: a pivot needs 10 bars on each side; bad wicks clamped). No depth bins: each pullback is a dot, placed by its depth and by how long it took to trade back above the old top. Pullbacks still under their old top stay on the chart as red rings at their wait so far. The curves group pullbacks by their rank among the instrument's own pullbacks (all, deeper half, deepest quarter, deepest tenth) — so “deep” means deep for that instrument, not a fixed percent.

4 · How each number is made, and where it comes from

RSI
RSI(14) with Wilder's smoothing on daily closes — the same function the Hub's statistics already use (research/statistics/stats.mjs). The first 100 readings of each series are left out as warm-up.
Rungs and the ladder
All counted days of an instrument are sorted by RSI; the number shown at rung q is the RSI below which q% of days closed. The “last 3 years” ladder uses the last 756 sessions (Bitcoin 1,095 days). A day's rung uses the whole history (hindsight); the no-hindsight column in each rung table ranks the day only against every earlier day (needs 250 earlier readings).
Visits
A visit to “rung q or lower” = a run of consecutive days at or below that rung's RSI. No merging of nearby visits.
What came next
Close-to-close change after 5/10/20/60 sessions (price only, no dividends; the 10-year yield in basis points). Worst close = the lowest close in the next 20 or 60 sessions against the day's close. Wait to prior top = sessions until the first day whose high trades above the most recent swing high already confirmed on that day (a swing high is only known 10 sessions after it prints); 0 if the day's own high is already above it. The middle wait uses Kaplan–Meier so days still waiting today are counted, not dropped.
90% bands
Cluster bootstrap, 1000 draws, fixed seed: whole calendar months of days are resampled for the 5/10/20-session numbers and whole calendar quarters for the 60-session numbers (their windows overlap across months).
Pullbacks
S9's swings: pivot highs and lows with 10 bars on each side on the wicks, forced to alternate, each leg end moved to the true extreme. Depth = low ÷ top − 1. “New high” = the first day whose high trades above the old top. Rallies needed = how many swing highs it took (1 = the very next one, S9's measure).

5 · What could be wrong

  • Hindsight in the rungs. A day's rung is set against the whole history, including years that came after it. The no-hindsight columns (each day ranked only against earlier days) are there to check; they differ most in the early years of each series.
  • Overlapping days. Neighbouring days share most of their forward window, so 57 rung-1 days of SPY are really about 21 separate months. The bands account for that by resampling whole months (quarters for 60 sessions); they may still be a little narrow when a stress lasted longer than a quarter.
  • Different histories. SPY starts in 2003, QQQ in 2011, the sectors in 2003 (XLRE 2015, XLC 2018), Bitcoin in 2013, the S&P index in 1928. Ladders built over different years are not strictly comparable; that is why the Bitcoin comparison uses the same years.
  • Bitcoin trades every day. Its 14-period RSI covers 14 calendar days; SPY's covers about 20. A weekday-only reading of Bitcoin gives the same ladder, but the RSI clock itself differs.
  • Early index data. The S&P history before the 1960s has close-only bars (high = low = close) and a few one-day prints that look like data faults (for example a −6.8% day on 16 May 1935 that fully reverses the next day). Pivots on those years use closes.
  • Oil below zero. WTI closed at −$37.63 on 20 April 2020; percent changes through a non-positive close are skipped and that pullback's depth is capped at −100% (marked *).
  • “Wait to prior top” is partly mechanical. On an oversold day price is usually far under the last swing high, so a long wait is expected; read it as a size of the hole, not as a signal.
  • Pullbacks in progress. A decline only becomes a pullback once its low is confirmed 10 bars later; anything falling right now is not in the list yet.
  • Prices, not total return. Dividends are not added, which understates long waits for the funds a little.

6 · What was not done

  • No trades, no alerts, no buy rules; nothing was written to any database, nothing was deployed.
  • No new downloads: every bar came from the existing statistics cache. The Russell 2000 and Dow index histories (1985–87→) are in that cache but were not added; IWM and DIA stand in for them.
  • No weekly or 4-hour RSI; daily only. No RSI divergence here (the separate RSI full-history page covers it).
  • Rung tables for the no-hindsight version give point results only, without bands.
  • Not yet on the Station or the Hub dashboard; this is a research page.
